content: A bachelor's degree is typically an undergraduate academic qualification awarded upon the completion of a program of study that generally spans three to four years, though in some countries and disciplines, it may extend to five or six years. In certain cases, the term bachelor's degree may also refer to postgraduate degrees, such as the Bachelor of Civil Law, Bachelor of Music, or Bachelor of Philosophy. In many English-speaking countries and those influenced by the English education system, undergraduate degrees are classified as either pass degrees or honours degrees. Honours degrees, often denoted by (Hons) after the degree abbreviation, require a higher academic standard than pass degrees. In some regions, such as Malta, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, Scotland, and South Africa, earning an honours degree may necessitate an additional year of study. Historically, in the UK, honours degrees required an extra year of study compared to ordinary degrees, a practice that still applies in Scotland for certain degrees like the MA (Hons). In England, most first degrees are now assumed to be honours degrees, as even the lowest classification, Third Class Honours, is considered a relatively modest academic achievement. However, some institutions, such as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), do not distinguish between honours and pass degrees, as they regard graduation itself as a significant accomplishment. In Canada, many universities no longer offer pass degrees, instead awarding honours degrees exclusively. For example, the University of Toronto, the largest university in Canada, follows this practice. In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, bachelor's degrees are awarded with designations such as BA (Bachelor of Arts), BSc (Bachelor of Science), or BEng (Bachelor of Engineering), depending on the subject area. Most bachelor's degrees are now honours degrees, classified into four categories based on final assessment and examination marks: First Class, Upper Second Class (2:1), Lower Second Class (2:2), and Third Class. Students who complete the full honours course but fail to meet the minimum requirements for a Third Class degree may be awarded an unclassified or ordinary degree. Ordinary degrees typically require fewer credits (300 CATS points) than honours degrees (360 CATS points) and may be awarded with distinction if the student's average marks exceed 70%. In Scotland, undergraduate degrees at the four ancient universities (St Andrews, Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Aberdeen) and Dundee are classified as either Designated Degrees or Honours Degrees. Honours degrees, such as the MA (Hons) for arts and social sciences or the BSc (Hons) for sciences, require four years of study, including two years at the sub-honours level and two years at the honours level, often culminating in a dissertation. Designated degrees, awarded after three years of study, involve less depth in the final year and do not typically include a dissertation. In the United States, bachelor's degrees are generally designed to be completed in four years of full-time study, though some programs, such as engineering or architecture, may take five years. Ambitious students may complete their degrees in as little as three years through summer school or advanced placement courses. Many U.S. institutions offer honours or scholars programs for top-performing students, which involve more challenging coursework or research projects. Graduates of these programs may receive a notation such as in cursu honorum on their diplomas. The most common bachelor's degrees worldwide are the Bachelor of Arts (BA) and Bachelor of Science (BSc). In the U.S., liberal arts colleges often award the BA for all academic subjects, while professional training programs may confer the BSc. Some institutions allow students to choose between a BA and a BSc in the same subject, with the BSc typically being more rigorous. Specialized bachelor's degrees exist in various fields, such as the Bachelor of Engineering (BEng), Bachelor of Architecture (BArch), Bachelor of Nursing (BN), and Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA). These degrees often require additional years of study or specific professional training. For example, the BArch typically takes five years to complete, while the BN prepares students for licensure as registered nurses. In Europe, bachelor's degrees were introduced or reintroduced in many countries as part of the Bologna Process, which standardized higher education across the continent. For instance, Austria and Denmark reintroduced bachelor's degrees in the early 2000s, with programs typically lasting three years. In Asia, bachelor's degree programs are modeled after Western systems, with durations ranging from three to five years depending on the field of study. In India, arts, commerce, and science colleges offer three-year bachelor's degrees, while engineering and medical programs require four to five years. Similarly, in Pakistan, bachelor's programs generally last four years, with engineering and architecture degrees taking five years. In the Philippines, bachelor's degrees are commonly referred to as courses and typically last four years, though some fields, such as architecture and engineering, require five years. Graduates may earn honors such as cum laude, magna cum laude, or summa cum laude, following the U.S. model. Overall, bachelor's degrees serve as foundational qualifications for further academic or professional pursuits, with variations in structure, duration, and specialization across different countries and disciplines.
